analysis.one_liner: Raises tipped workers' base pay to the full federal minimum wage and stops employers from keeping tips.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in either committee or on the House floor, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, after 10 Democratic House members sponsored it.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets restaurants pay tipped workers as little as $2.13 an hour in cash, on the theory that tips will cover the rest. This bill would eliminate that separate lower wage: tipped workers' cash pay would rise from $3.60 an hour by $1.50 each year until it reached the full federal minimum wage. It would also bar employers from keeping any tips or using them to cover credit card processing fees, give workers the right to vote on whether to pool tips, and require businesses to disclose and pass along mandatory service charges to employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Tipped workers — servers, bartenders, salon workers, and others whose employers pay the low federal tipped minimum — get a guaranteed rising cash wage until it reaches the federal minimum, regardless of how their tips fall. They also keep every tip they earn, can't have tips clawed back to cover card fees, and can force a vote on tip-pooling rules.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the separate tipped minimum wage: employers' required cash wage for tipped employees rises from $3.60 an hour by $1.50 each year until it equals the federal minimum wage under section 6(a)(1).
Bars employers from keeping any tips or using them for any purpose except distributing them to workers, and specifically bans using tips to cover debit or credit card transaction fees.

Gives workers a vote: if 30% of a workplace's non-supervisory employees request one and 51% vote yes, a tip pool must be established, with voluntary participation and a ban on employers punishing workers over the vote.

Requires businesses that impose mandatory service charges to tell customers and workers what portion goes to employees and to pay that portion directly to them promptly, and treats that portion as tips for payroll tax purposes.

analysis.who_pays: Restaurant, hotel, and personal-service employers who currently pay the $2.13 federal tipped minimum would pay several dollars more per hour in guaranteed cash wages, and would give up practices like keeping service charges or netting card fees out of tips. Costs would likely be passed to customers through higher prices or service charges.

drawbacks.text: Opponents of ending the tipped wage typically argue that requiring employers to pay the full minimum in cash raises restaurant labor costs enough to lead to higher menu prices, fewer hours, or job cuts that fall on the same workers the bill aims to help.
The bill only raises tipped workers' cash wage up to the existing federal minimum of $7.25 an hour; it does not raise that minimum, so even when fully phased in the guarantee is low.
The tip-pool provisions let the employer administer the pool and impose a resolution of disputes among employees, which some workers could find gives the employer too much control over shared tips.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is a real wage guarantee for roughly the lowest-paid group of workers in the country, replacing a system where a bad night of tips can leave a worker legally paid $2.13 an hour. The main cost is higher labor costs for restaurants, likely passed to customers in prices; whether that cost is worth the guarantee is the honest tradeoff, and the bill's phase-in over several years was designed to soften it. The bill's weakness is that it tops out at $7.25 an hour, a wage that is itself widely considered too low.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in September 2023 and referred to two House committees, but neither committee ever held a hearing or voted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jahana Hayes introduced the Tipped Worker Protection Act on September 8, 2023, with eight Democratic cosponsors joining as original sponsors.

The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and the Workforce and to the Committee on Ways and Means; the record shows no markup, hearing, or vote in either committee after the referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the $2.13 federal tipped minimum wage keep the current system, and tipped workers keep waiting for a guaranteed cash wage.

for.name: Rep. Jahana Hayes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the tipped minimum wage and wrote its phase-in from $3.60 an hour to the full federal minimum.

for.name: 8 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors (Bonamici, Schakowsky, Titus, Thompson of MS, Carter of LA, Bowman, Watson Coleman, Jackson of IL)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors on the day of introduction; no further recorded action.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction with a Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but never held a markup or moved the bill in the 15 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for its tax provisions but took no recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never got to a roll call, so no vote breakdown exists.

industries.note: Restaurants would have to pay tipped staff several dollars more per hour in guaranteed cash wages as the phase-in reached the full federal minimum. Their interest in keeping the $2.13 tipped minimum runs directly against the wage guarantee workers would gain.

industries.industry: Hotels, salons, and other businesses using mandatory service charges
industries.note: The bill requires these businesses to disclose what portion of a mandatory service charge goes to employees and to hand that portion over promptly, ending their ability to retain service charges. Customers also gain clarity about where their money goes.

The bill explicitly bans employers from covering debit and credit card transaction fees out of employees' tips, shifting that cost fully onto businesses and, indirectly, prices. The effect is small relative to the wage provisions.
